title: Why Landfills Emit Methane and How Kitchen Segregation Stops It
summary: When food waste is dumped inside plastic bags, it decomposes anaerobically without oxygen, producing methane gas (CH₄)—a greenhouse pollutant 28x more potent than carbon dioxide over a 20-year horizon. Segregating wet waste allows aerobic decomposition into compost, cutting landfill fire risks and turning city waste into nutrient-dense soil conditioner.
takeaways: Anaerobic landfill decomposition creates flammable methane pockets.
Aerobic home or society composting yields zero foul odor when balanced 2:1 with dry carbon leaves.
Every 1 kg of wet waste composted averts ~1.26 kg of greenhouse emissions.

title: The Lifecycle of a PET Bottle: How Clean Rinsing Multiplies Recycler Value
summary: PET (Polyethylene Terephthalate) is 100% recyclable into polyester yarn, sports apparel, and secondary packaging—but only if not contaminated with grease or food oils. When you rinse and crush your bottles, informal eco-pickers earn 40% higher market rates from mechanized material recovery facilities (MRFs).
takeaways: Unwashed bottles often get rejected at sorting centers and diverted back to landfills.
Crushing bottles reduces transport volume by 70%, slashing collection truck diesel fuel.
Keep bottle caps inside or screwed loosely so small parts don't slip through conveyor screens.

title: Old Phone Chargers & Wires: The Urban Copper Mine in Your Drawer
summary: Electronic cables contain high-purity electrolytic copper and tin shielded by PVC. When burned illegally or dumped, they release toxic dioxins and lead into local water tables. Diverting just 1 metric ton of cables yields ~400 kg of copper, using 85% less energy than mining virgin chalcopyrite copper ore.
takeaways: Never snip or burn wire insulation at home; authorized recyclers use cold mechanical granulators.
Copper is infinitely recyclable without losing electrical conductivity.
Store cables dry; moisture oxidizes copper connectors and lowers recycling grade.

title: Balcony Composting: The 2:1 Golden Rule for Odor-Free Apartments
summary: Urban composting fails only when moisture is too high. The secret is the 'Brown to Green' balance: 2 handfuls of dry brown carbon (crushed dry leaves, egg cartons, shredded newspaper) for every 1 handful of wet kitchen greens (vegetable peels, tea bags, fruit skins). Turn it once a week for fresh, forest-scented compost.
takeaways: Browns provide structure and air channels; greens provide moisture and nitrogen.
Avoid dairy, cooked oils, and meat in small balcony pots to prevent fruit flies.
Sprinkle a handful of garden soil or sour buttermilk to jumpstart beneficial microbial bacteria.

title: Expired Medicines & Sanitary Items: Why the Red/Black Bin Matters
summary: Flushing antibiotics down the toilet causes antimicrobial resistance in municipal water rivers, while dumping sanitary waste into compost bins spreads pathogens to field workers. The designated Landfill/Hazardous stream ensures high-temperature biomedical incineration and safe scientific containment.
takeaways: Never flush antibiotics, pain killers, or syrups down household sinks.
Wrap sanitary pads in marked newspaper before disposal to protect eco-picker dignity.
Keep blister strip medicines separate from standard dry paper packaging.

title: What Is the Circular Economy? Moving from 'Take-Make-Waste' to Closed Loops
summary: In the traditional linear economy, raw natural resources are extracted, processed into goods, and discarded after single use. A circular economy keeps materials cycling at their highest economic utility forever through reuse, refurbishment, and clean remanufacturing, decoupling human prosperity from natural resource depletion.
takeaways: Circularity designs out waste before products are even manufactured.
Source segregation is the critical first link connecting homes to manufacturing mills.
Every eco-credit you earn on IndoHood represents raw materials kept in active use.
